6.title: Not actually a Dragon
6.text: Despite the wings, horns and fire breath, Charizard is Fire/Flying and has never been a Dragon type. That is why Dragon Rage never got the boost fans expected — and why a single Rock throw hurts it four times over.

25.title: Its name is a sound effect
25.text: In Japanese, pika is the crackle of electricity and chu is the squeak a mouse makes. Pikachu is literally 'spark-squeak' — the designers named it after the noise it makes.

37.title: Born from the kitsune
37.text: Vulpix and Ninetales come from the kitsune of Japanese folklore: foxes that grow an extra tail every century, gaining wisdom and magic with each one. Nine tails means the fox has reached its final, most powerful form.

38.title: A thousand-year grudge
38.text: Kitsune legends warn that harming a nine-tailed fox invites a curse that lasts a thousand years — which is exactly what Ninetales' Pokédex entries say happens if you pull one of its tails.

47.title: A real-life zombie fungus
47.text: Parasect is based on Ophiocordyceps, a fungus that infects insects and steers their bodies before sprouting from them. Its blank white eyes are not a design quirk — the mushroom is the one in control now.

50.title: What is under a Diglett?
50.text: Fans have argued for decades about whether Diglett has legs, a full body, or nothing at all. Game Freak has teased the question for years without ever giving a straight answer, making it one of the longest-running mysteries in the series.

65.title: The lawsuit over a spoon
65.text: Kadabra's Japanese name, Yungerer, references the performer Uri Geller, famous for bending spoons. Geller sued Nintendo in 2000, and Kadabra vanished from the trading card game for roughly two decades — until Geller publicly apologised to fans in 2020 and granted permission to use it again.

79.title: A bite that changes everything
79.text: Slowpoke does not evolve by level. A Shellder clamps onto its tail and refuses to let go, and the shock turns the dopey Slowpoke into Slowbro. Bite the head instead and you get Slowking, who becomes remarkably clever.

83.title: A duck carrying its own seasoning
83.text: Farfetch'd comes from the Japanese proverb kamo ga negi wo shotte kuru — 'a duck comes carrying a spring onion' — meaning something almost too convenient to be true. That is also where the English name comes from: it is a far-fetched story.

88.title: Born from pollution
88.text: Grimer is officially sludge brought to life by industrial waste and X-ray exposure from the moon. It was designed during a period when Japan was reckoning with severe industrial pollution, and its Pokédex entries read like environmental warnings.

94.title: Clefable's shadow
94.text: One of the oldest fan theories in the series: Gengar's silhouette lines up almost perfectly with Clefable's, and Gengar is described as a shadow that mimics and follows people. Fans argue Gengar is Clefable's own shadow come loose. Game Freak has never confirmed it, but nobody has quite let the idea go either.

96.title: The dream eater
96.text: Drowzee is based on the baku, a Japanese spirit said to devour nightmares. Traditionally you called on a baku after a bad dream — but the legends warn that a hungry baku might eat your hopes and dreams along with the nightmare.

100.title: A Poké Ball that woke up
100.text: Voltorb looks exactly like an upside-down Poké Ball, and it first appeared around the time Poké Ball manufacturing began. The popular fan explanation is that Voltorb is a Poké Ball brought to life by an electrical accident — the games only ever say it 'appeared' at a Poké Ball factory.

104.title: The orphan and the skull
104.text: Cubone wears the skull of its dead mother and cries beneath it. The most famous fan theory says Cubone is an orphaned baby Kangaskhan — which is why nobody ever sees a Kangaskhan baby leave the pouch. It fits the mood of Lavender Town disturbingly well, though it has never been confirmed.

109.title: Smokestacks in a mask
109.text: Galarian Weezing wears what look like Victorian factory chimneys and a gentleman's moustache — a nod to Britain's industrial revolution. In a neat twist, this version purifies the polluted air it inhales instead of spreading it.

115.title: The baby that never leaves
115.text: Kangaskhan's child never appears as its own Pokémon, never battles separately, and has no separate entry. That empty space in the dex is exactly what feeds the Cubone theory.

129.title: The carp that became a dragon
129.text: A Chinese legend tells of carp that swim up a waterfall called the Dragon Gate; any that make the leap are transformed into dragons. Magikarp is that carp — flopping and useless until it endures long enough to become Gyarados.

130.title: The reward for persistence
130.text: Gyarados is the other half of the Dragon Gate legend — the fish that made the leap. There is a joke buried in it too: after all that struggle, it comes out Water/Flying rather than the Dragon type everyone expects.

131.title: The Loch Ness Monster
131.text: Lapras is a plesiosaur, the long-necked shape people claim to see in Loch Ness. Its dex entries lean into the same melancholy: a gentle, intelligent creature hunted to near-extinction and now rarely sighted.

132.title: The failed Mew clone
132.text: Ditto and Mew weigh exactly the same, both learn Transform, both are pink, and in Red and Blue both appear around the Pokémon Mansion where the Mewtwo experiments went wrong. The theory: Ditto is a Mew clone that did not hold its shape. The evidence is circumstantial — but it is a lot of coincidences.

133.title: Named after its own gimmick
133.text: Eevee's name comes from the letters E-V, for evolution, and its unstable genetic code is the in-universe reason it can branch into so many forms. It has more evolutions than any other Pokémon.

137.title: Blamed for something it did not do
137.text: A 1997 episode caused seizures in hundreds of viewers in Japan. The flashing came from Pikachu's attack, not Porygon — yet Porygon and both its evolutions have never appeared in another episode since.

143.title: Modelled on a colleague
143.text: Snorlax is widely reported to be based on Game Freak developer Kōji Nishino, known around the office for eating and then promptly falling asleep.

150.title: The diary in the ruins
150.text: You can read the story of Mewtwo's creation on abandoned journals in the Pokémon Mansion on Cinnabar Island. The entries record Mew giving birth, the experiments that followed, and then simply stop — one of the first times a Pokémon game told a genuinely dark story through scenery alone.

151.title: Smuggled in at the last minute
151.text: Mew was not in the plan. Programmer Shigeki Morimoto slipped it into Red and Green in leftover memory after debug features were removed, without telling management. It was never meant to be obtainable — which is exactly how the schoolyard rumours about the truck near the S.S. Anne began.

185.title: A terrible disguise
185.text: Sudowoodo pretends to be a tree, but its arms are the wrong shape, it stays green in winter when real trees turn bare, and it hates water. It is a Rock type doing an extremely unconvincing impression of a plant.

202.title: Its tail is the real one
202.text: The black tail with eyes is Wobbuffet's actual body, and it will hide that tail at all costs. The blue part everyone thinks of as Wobbuffet is closer to a decoy.

249.title: Guardian of the sea
249.text: Lugia's design borrows from both a plesiosaur and the beluga whale, and its role echoes Japanese sea-guardian myths — a creature so powerful it must stay hidden at the bottom of the ocean to avoid destroying what it protects.

250.title: The phoenix on the tower
250.text: Ho-Oh is a phoenix, and its home, the Bell Tower, mirrors Kyoto's golden Kinkaku-ji temple which is crowned by a phoenix statue. Ho-Oh's Rainbow Wing and its habit of resurrecting the dead both fit the legend it came from.

289.title: Wasted potential, by design
289.text: Slaking has monstrous base stats — higher than many legendaries — but its Truant ability forces it to skip every other turn. It is a deliberate joke: the strongest lazy Pokémon in the game, balanced by simply not bothering.

321.title: Lighter than it looks
321.text: Wailord is the longest Pokémon in the dex at 14.5 metres, yet it weighs less than many Pokémon a fraction of its size. Run the numbers and it turns out to be less dense than water — which is why it floats so easily.

359.title: Blamed for the disaster it warned about
359.text: Absol senses coming earthquakes and storms and comes down from the mountains to warn people — who then assume it caused them. It is a tidy retelling of how real folklore turns unlucky omens into villains.

425.title: Do not take its hand
425.text: This one is not a fan theory. Drifloon's official entries say it tugs at children's hands to lead them away, and that it is rumoured to be formed from the souls of people and Pokémon. The games say it out loud.

442.title: One hundred and eight spirits
442.text: Spiritomb is 108 spirits bound to an Odd Keystone — and 108 is the number of earthly desires in Buddhist tradition, the same number of times temple bells ring on New Year's Eve. Fittingly, catching one in Diamond and Pearl required talking to 32 other players underground.

448.title: The jackal that reads you
448.text: Lucario's head and ears come from Anubis, the jackal-headed Egyptian god who weighed the hearts of the dead. Lucario's aura sense — reading emotions and intentions — is the same idea in gentler clothing.

562.title: It used to be a person
562.text: Yamask carries a mask of the human face it had before it died, and its entries say it sometimes looks at the mask and cries. This is official text in a game rated for children.

563.title: A sarcophagus with an appetite
563.text: Cofagrigus is an Egyptian sarcophagus that swallows grave robbers and turns them into more Cofagrigus. Real tomb curses were inscribed to scare looters away — this one simply handles the problem itself.

623.title: A golem with a seal
623.text: Golurk is an automaton animated by a sealed core, echoing the Jewish golem legend where a clay figure is brought to life by a written word. Its entries say removing the seal on its chest stops it instantly.

707.title: A fairy that steals keys
707.text: Klefki collects keys and refuses to hand them over, which comes from the European habit of hanging iron keys as charms against evil spirits. Being a Steel/Fairy type is the joke: it is a fairy made of the very metal fairies are supposed to fear.

778.title: It just wants to be loved
778.text: Mimikyu wears a homemade Pikachu rag because Pikachu merchandise was popular and it wanted friends too. Its entries also state that anyone who sees what is under the cloth dies of shock — both things are official.

890.title: The biggest number in the dex
890.text: Eternatus has 690 total base stats, beaten only by Arceus, and at 20 metres and 950 kg it is both the tallest and heaviest Pokémon on record. Its energy core is literally the power source the whole Galar crisis runs on.
